data.name: Virus Jigglin' Fever
data.detailed_description:
During an exclusive tour of the "Science Lab of Creating Viruses that can Murder the hell out of Humanity for Science Reasons" an excitable Australian broke a vial, labeled "The Good Stuff". It unleashed some of the deadliest viruses known to humankind...

Dr. Boffpow, the not senile scientist sprung into action creating an "extremely viable" solution to the outbreak.

The Virus Scanner, which shows where viruses are located.
The Virus Magnifier, a glass box that contains and magnifies the viruses.
A ball of drugs. Similar to a bouncy ball, but with pharmaceutical goodness.
"This... thing?" a paddle that changes the ball of drugs to cure different types of viruses.
You are the key member of a team of self-proclaimed virus killers formed to save the planet. Control the paddle thing and destroy the virus outbreak!

FEATURING:
Arcade-style game experience!
Multiple difficulties including endless mode!
Viruses with unique personalities!
Play with keyboard, controller, or touchscreen!
Two different modes of touch input, including virtual controller!

CREDITS:
Game Art, Story, Lead Design: Chloe Sagal (@chloesagal)
Programming & Design: Cecelia Wren (@satsukitv)
Design: Lexi Leigh Richardson (@lexi_like_crazy)
Story Art: Frank Stringini
Music: Bit by Bit Sound (@BitByBitSound)

reviews.review:
Virus Jigglin' Fever is a lazy port of what appears to be a pretty decent mobile game.  When I first wrote this review the price was a whopping $5, but it's now been lowered to $2 to match the mobile version, so kudos to the devs for that.

The gameplay is a take on the "breakout" arcade game.  You must bounce balls to destroy the viruses (blocks), but the ball must be the same color as the virus it hits in order to clear it, and the ball changes color each time it bounces off your paddle.  The paddle is actually carried by the pixelated little person you control, and instead of freely moving and stopping as in most games of this genre, you move between 5 levels.  By default the paddle is not large enough to cover an entire level, so often you must time your move between the levels to be able to keep the ball in play.

There are the usual assortment of power-ups, and hitting some viruses with a wrong colored ball can have mildly unpleasant side effects.  Some userfriendly touches involve a helpful display letting you know the color the ball will become after the next bounce so that you can plan ahead, the ball only cycling through colors of viruses which are still present in the level (bust-a-move style), and the rapid delivery of "split ball" power-ups once there are only 1 or 2 viruses left.  

Annoyingly, one "power-up" actually makes it easier to miss the ball, by obscuring the area immediately around the paddle with thick colored arrows dynamically moving to point to any balls in play.  I can see those balls just fine, thank-you-very-much, but not when they're being covered by the arrows!

The story campaign consists of multiple zones of 3 levels each.  You have 3 balls to complete each level, after which you must start the level over.  There are unlimited such retries, but the game only saves progress after you've completed a zone, so if you are on the third level of a zone when you decide to quit, you'll have to repeat the first two levels again next time.  As you proceed through the campaign, additional virus colors are added to raise the difficulty.

The graphics are pretty decent "8-bit retro" style, as can be seen in the screenshots.  What's not apparent from the screenshots is that the game launches in a tiny 640x480 window, and the only other option is to stretch it all the way to Full Screen with ALT+ENTER (something the game assumes you already know to do, as it's not mentioned anywhere.)   You'll have to do it again every time you start the game.  The framerate is locked to 30fps, but that's not a problem in a game like this with no scrolling, and I didn't notice any input lag.  

There are multiple difficulty settings, as well as an endless mode, but I couldn't figure out how to actually activate them.  The spacebar is used to switch the other settings in the menu, but did nothing here - are these locked out until you beat the campaign on the default difficulty?  Who knows - the game certainly doesn't tell you.

The short cutscenes are amusing, but I found the text, being both highly pixelated and italicized, annoyingly hard to read.

The music is very good chiptune, but doesn't have much variety.

And then we come to the interface.  The only consideration made for PC users in this port is the ability to use the keyboard, and enable an xinput controller (such as my 360 pad), neither remappable.  You can also awkwardly control movement with the mouse, but cannot launch the ball by clicking, so that's pretty much  useless.  There is an option to overlay the screen with control prompts, but it is absolutely hideous, and covers too much of the screen.   Without such prompts, you don't even know how to exit to the menu from inside the level.  Escape (keyboard)/ Start (360 controller) bring up the Pause screen, and pressing them again resumes the gameplay - you somehow have to figure out to hit Backspace / B from the Pause menu in order to actually quit the level.

And of course there are no Steamworks features, not even achievements which are usually expected in arcade games.

So in the end, I can't recommend a game that's optimized for touch controls and offers no PC specific changes beyond the base ability to use a keyboard or a controller.
